section.title: Samson's Revenge
section.sectionRationale: The lost bride sets off a chain of escalating revenge. Samson burns the Philistine harvest with foxes and firebrands; they burn his wife and her father; he strikes them in slaughter; they invade Judah to seize him; his own countrymen bind him and hand him over; and the Spirit rushes on him so that with a donkey's jawbone he kills a thousand. Then, near death from thirst, he cries to the LORD and God gives water. One movement holds together human vengeance and divine deliverance.
section.thesis: Personal revenge spirals into open war, yet through Samson's flawed vengeance the LORD grants Israel a great deliverance, and the thirsty deliverer learns that his strength and his very life are gifts he must ask of God.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the foxes and the burning fields, verses 1 to 5; blood for blood, verses 6 to 8; Judah binds its own deliverer, verses 9 to 13; the jawbone and the thousand, verses 14 to 17; and the cry for water at En-hakkore, verses 18 to 20.

units.label: The foxes and the burning fields

verses.text: Later on, at the time of the wheat harvest, Samson took a young goat and went to visit his wife. “I want to go to my wife in her room,” he said. But her father would not let him enter.
“I was sure that you thoroughly hated her,” said her father, “so I gave her to one of the men who accompanied you. Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she? Please take her instead.”
Samson said to them, “This time I will be blameless in doing harm to the Philistines.”
Then Samson went out and caught three hundred foxes. And he took torches, turned the foxes tail-to-tail, and fastened a torch between each pair of tails.
Then he lit the torches and released the foxes into the standing grain of the Philistines, burning up the piles of grain and the standing grain, as well as the vineyards and olive groves.

units.label: Blood for blood
units.note: I will not rest until I have taken vengeance

verses.text: “Who did this?” the Philistines demanded. “It was Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite,” they were told. “For his wife was given to his companion.” So the Philistines went up and burned her and her father to death.
And Samson told them, “Because you have done this, I will not rest until I have taken {{naqam|vengeance}} upon you.”
And he struck them ruthlessly with a great slaughter, and then went down and stayed in the cave at the rock of Etam.

units.label: Judah binds its deliverer
units.note: do you not realize the Philistines rule over us

verses.text: Then the Philistines went up, camped in Judah, and deployed themselves near the town of Lehi.
“Why have you attacked us?” said the men of Judah. The Philistines replied, “We have come to arrest Samson and pay him back for what he has done to us.”

In response, three thousand men of Judah went to the cave at the rock of Etam, and they asked Samson, “Do you not realize that the Philistines rule over us? What have you done to us?” “I have done to them what they did to me,” he replied.
But they said to him, “We have come down to arrest you and hand you over to the Philistines.” Samson replied, “Swear to me that you will not kill me yourselves.”
“No,” they answered, “we will not kill you, but we will tie you up securely and hand you over to them.” So they bound him with two new ropes and led him up from the rock.

When Samson arrived in Lehi, the Philistines came out shouting against him. And the {{ruach|Spirit}} of the LORD came mightily upon him. The ropes on his arms became like burnt flax, and the bonds broke loose from his hands.
He found the fresh {{lechi|jawbone}} of a donkey, reached out his hand and took it, and struck down a thousand men.
Then Samson said: “With the jawbone of a donkey I have piled them into heaps. With the jawbone of a donkey I have slain a thousand men.”
And when Samson had finished speaking, he cast the jawbone from his hand; and he named that place Ramath-lehi.

units.label: The cry for water at En-hakkore
units.note: must I now die of thirst

verses.text: And being very thirsty, Samson cried out to the LORD, “You have accomplished this great {{teshuah|deliverance}} through Your servant. Must I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?”

So God opened up the hollow place in Lehi, and water came out of it. When Samson drank, his strength returned, and he was revived. That is why he named it En-hakkore, and it remains in Lehi to this day.
And Samson judged Israel for twenty years in the days of the Philistines.

ruach.gloss: Spirit, breath, wind. As in chapter 14, the ruach of the LORD comes mightily on Samson, verse 14, snapping his ropes like burnt flax so that he strikes down a thousand men. The Spirit is the true source of the deliverance, working through a man who is acting largely out of personal revenge, so that the victory is God's gift rather than Samson's achievement.

naqam.gloss: Vengeance, revenge, requital. Samson's cry, I will not rest until I have taken naqam, verse 7, drives the whole chapter's escalating cycle of retaliation. In Scripture vengeance ultimately belongs to God, Deuteronomy 32:35; Samson takes it into his own hands, and though God uses the result to strike the Philistines, the personal, appetite-driven revenge is portrayed honestly as flawed.

lechi.gloss: Jawbone; also the place name Lehi. Samson kills a thousand with the fresh lechi of a donkey, an unclean and unlikely weapon, then names the place Ramath-lehi, the hill of the jawbone. The wordplay ties weapon and place together and underlines the theme that God saves by weak and improbable means, not by conventional strength or arms.

teshuah.gloss: Deliverance, salvation, victory. In verse 18 Samson himself names his feat God's teshuah, this great deliverance accomplished through Your servant. The word reframes the slaughter: it was not merely Samson's revenge but God's saving act for Israel, and Samson's admission that his strength and life depend wholly on the LORD who granted it.

basic.context: After the wedding disaster of chapter 14, Samson returns to claim his wife, only to learn her father has given her to another. Declaring himself blameless, he burns the Philistines' harvest by tying torches to three hundred foxes. The Philistines retaliate by burning his wife and her father to death, the very fate she had once feared. Samson strikes them in a great slaughter, then hides at the rock of Etam. The Philistines invade Judah to seize him, and three thousand men of Judah, resigned to Philistine rule, bind their own deliverer and hand him over. But the Spirit of the LORD rushes on him; he breaks free, seizes a donkey's jawbone, and kills a thousand men. Then, dying of thirst, he cries to the LORD, who splits open a spring, and Samson revives. He judges Israel twenty years.
basic.hermeneutics: This is honest history of a cycle of revenge, told without whitewashing. Samson's motives are largely personal, tit-for-tat retaliation, and the narrator does not commend the appetite for vengeance that drives him. Yet the same story shows the Spirit granting a real deliverance and God answering a desperate prayer with mercy. We must not read Samson's private revenge as a model, nor deny that God genuinely worked through it to rescue His people and to teach His servant dependence.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter turns on four words. The ruach, the Spirit of the LORD, rushes on Samson, verse 14, and is the true power behind the victory. Samson's cry for naqam, vengeance, verse 7, drives the escalating cycle, though vengeance belongs to God. He kills a thousand with a lechi, a jawbone, then names the place after it, showing God saving by weak means. And Samson finally calls the whole event God's teshuah, deliverance, admitting his strength was a gift.
basic.typology: Samson is a deliverer who saves Israel, is handed over to the enemy by his own people, yet triumphs, and in this he faintly foreshadows Christ, who was delivered up by His own nation but conquered. The improbable weapon and the water given in the place of death also point, however dimly, to a God who saves through weakness and gives living water to the dying.
basic.christ: Samson's own countrymen, resigned to their bondage, bind him and hand him to the enemy, yet through that handing over comes deliverance. So the Lord Jesus was delivered up by His own people to the powers of this world, yet through that very handing over He won salvation. Where Samson took vengeance and killed his enemies, Christ, the greater Deliverer, bore vengeance in Himself and prayed for His enemies, conquering not by slaughter but by His death. And the water God gave the dying Samson points to Christ, who gives living water so we never thirst.
basic.god: The chapter reveals a God who is sovereign over human vengeance, weaving even Samson's flawed retaliation into a real deliverance for His people. He empowers by His Spirit, He saves by unlikely means, a jawbone rather than an army, and He is tender to His exhausted servant, hearing his cry and opening a spring. God is shown to be both the true author of the deliverance and the merciful giver of life to the one who calls on Him.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 32 declares that vengeance belongs to God. Romans 12 tells believers never to avenge themselves but to leave room for God's wrath. John 4 and 7 present Christ as the giver of living water. And Judges 15:14 shows the Spirit rushing on the deliverer, the pattern of the judges.
basic.oneStory: In an age when Israel was content in its chains, God raised a flawed deliverer and worked through his very vengeance to strike the oppressor and rescue His people. The Spirit empowered him, unlikely means won the day, and a dying man was revived by God's mercy. It is one more step in the long story of God saving through weak instruments, pointing to Christ, the Deliverer handed over by His own, who conquers through death and gives living water.

context.literary:
The chapter continues the Samson cycle with a tightly linked chain of cause and effect: each act of revenge provokes the next. The motif of fire runs through it, the burned harvest and the burned wife, and the improbable weapons, foxes and a jawbone, mark Samson as a wild, unconventional deliverer. The closing scene shifts abruptly from slaughter to a prayer of weakness, and the naming of Ramath-lehi and En-hakkore fixes the events in the land's memory.

The plot advances almost entirely through a chain of exact retaliation, each clause answering the one before it with a because or a so that leaves no room between one act and the next: because his wife was given away, he burns their fields; because their fields were burned, they burn her and her father; because they were burned, he strikes them with a great slaughter. No judge story in the book moves with this kind of mechanical, blow for blow causality. Fire itself becomes an ironic thread, the very weapon Samson turns against Philistine crops returning against his own family by the same method. The scene also widens the story's frame for a moment beyond Samson himself: three thousand men of Judah appear, the first time an entire tribe's fear, not just one man's temper, drives the plot, exposing a nation so reconciled to servitude that it will hand over its own deliverer to keep the peace. The chapter closes with a small prayer of complaint and thirst answered, En-hakkore, a shape close to the individual laments of the Psalms compressed into a single narrative beat.
context.historical:
The wheat harvest was the Philistines' vital food supply, so burning the standing grain, vineyards, and olive groves struck at their economy. Judah, under Philistine domination, had grown so accustomed to servitude that they policed their own deliverer to keep the peace. Lehi lay in the Judean foothills; naming sites after events, as with Ramath-lehi and En-hakkore, was a common way to preserve their significance.

The Hebrew word for the animals Samson catches can denote either foxes or jackals, and jackals, which run in packs and were a common pest in Judean vineyards, may make better sense of catching three hundred of them than solitary foxes would. The rock of Etam where Samson hides, like the many limestone caves throughout the Judean hill country, offered natural refuge from an armed and organized enemy that outmatched Israel militarily; three thousand unarmed men of Judah facing a garrisoned Philistine force explains, without excusing, their eagerness to hand over one troublesome man rather than fight. The text is careful to specify that the jawbone Samson seizes was fresh, verse 15, still moist rather than sun bleached and brittle, which is exactly what would let it serve as a weapon at all rather than shattering on the first blow, a small realistic detail that grounds the scene's extravagant violence in an ordinary fact about bone.
context.canonical:
Samson stands late in the downward spiral of Judges, when even Israel's own tribe would rather hand over its deliverer than be free. This tragic passivity exposes the nation's need for a true King and Saviour. The Spirit-empowered deliverance and the answered prayer belong to the pattern of the judges, while the handing over of the deliverer by his own people anticipates, at a great distance, the betrayal and triumph of Christ.

The pattern of one man standing alone against the whole Philistine army recurs later at its most famous, when a young David faces Goliath while the rest of Israel's forces stand back in fear, 1 Samuel 17:11, showing that the deliverance this chapter models, a single Spirit-strengthened figure doing what an entire discouraged nation will not, is not unique to Samson but becomes a recognizable shape of how God saves Israel from the Philistines across an entire generation. The naming of En-hakkore also belongs to a wider biblical habit of marking a place forever by what God did there, as Jacob names Peniel after wrestling with God, Genesis 32:30, and Bethel after his vision of the ladder, Genesis 28:19; Israel's map itself becomes a kind of testimony, so that later generations walking past a spring in Lehi were meant to remember a defeated enemy and an answered prayer, not merely a convenient water source.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
To show God granting Israel a real deliverance through Samson's flawed vengeance, to expose Judah's shameful contentment in bondage, and to teach, through the cry at En-hakkore, that even the mighty deliverer depends wholly on the LORD for strength and life.

The writer wants his hearers to feel the shame of Judah's three thousand men before they feel any admiration for Samson's strength; a tribe that negotiates the surrender of its own deliverer rather than risk a fight has already lost something no military defeat could take from it, a willingness to be free. By placing that scene at the center of the chapter, framed on both sides by Samson's private acts of retaliation, the author teaches that God's deliverance in this era does not depend on a united, courageous nation but works despite a fearful and complicit one. The closing prayer for water carries its own separate lesson, aimed less at Israel's politics than at Samson's own heart: the same man who has just killed a thousand men single handed is shown, within verses, unable to supply his own next drink, so that hearers are meant to conclude that even the greatest deliverer is still only a dependent creature before the LORD who gave him everything he has.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The narrative describes Samson's escalating personal revenge; it does not prescribe it. His tit-for-tat retaliation is honestly portrayed, not held up as a pattern for God's people, whom Scripture commands to leave vengeance to God. What endures is God's sovereign use of the situation, His strength by weak means, and His mercy to the one who calls on Him.

It is worth noticing what the text does not say as much as what it does. Samson is never commended in this chapter for burning fields or slaughtering men in anger; the narrator simply records his words, I will not rest until I have taken vengeance, without a single word of divine approval attached to them. That silence is itself instructive: Scripture can report an action accurately and let its consequences, an entire people group drawn into war, speak the verdict rather than stating one outright. What is transferable is the shape of Samson's last act rather than his first ones, a desperate, honest prayer from a position of total weakness, since dependence on God for one's very breath is commanded of every believer in every generation, not only of Nazirites at the end of their strength.

debates.question: How do God's sovereign deliverance and Samson's sinful vengeance relate in this chapter?

views.label: God overrules the vengeance without endorsing it
views.case: Scripture reserves vengeance for God, Deuteronomy 32:35, so Samson's personal retaliation is not commended. Yet the Spirit genuinely empowers him and God grants a real deliverance, showing that the LORD can accomplish His saving purpose through flawed and even sinful human acts without approving the sin in them.

views.label: Samson acts, in part, as God's appointed agent of judgment
views.case: Because Samson was raised up specifically to strike the Philistines, some see his blows as a form of divinely sanctioned judgment on an oppressing enemy, so that his actions carry a genuine, if imperfect, judicial role in God's dealings with the Philistines.

debates.bearing: Holding the first as primary keeps us from baptizing personal revenge; God's use of Samson's deeds is providence, not permission. It assures us God can bring good even from tangled motives, while still calling us to leave vengeance to Him.

debates.question: What is the point of Samson's prayer and near-death from thirst at En-hakkore?

views.label: A lesson in the deliverer's dependence
views.case: Immediately after his greatest triumph, Samson is helpless with thirst and must cry to God, who alone gave the victory. The scene deflates any self-reliance: the same strength that killed a thousand cannot make water, teaching that Samson's power and very life are gifts from the LORD.

views.label: Evidence of real, if immature, faith
views.case: Samson rightly names the victory God's deliverance through His servant and calls on the LORD in his need; the answered prayer shows a genuine, though undeveloped, relationship with God beneath the bravado.

debates.bearing: Both readings humble and encourage: the strongest are still utterly dependent on God, and God graciously hears even a flawed servant's honest cry, giving water to the thirsty.

study.originalLanguages:
Four words carry the chapter. The engine of the plot is naqam, vengeance: I will not rest until I have taken vengeance upon you, verse 7. In Scripture vengeance belongs to the LORD, Deuteronomy 32:35, and the narrator lets us feel how Samson's private, appetite-driven revenge sets off an escalating cycle of fire and blood, honestly shown as flawed even as God uses it. The turning point is the ruach, the Spirit of the LORD, who comes mightily on Samson, verse 14, so that ropes fall away like burnt flax; the deliverance is plainly the Spirit's doing, not Samson's own. God's chosen weapon is a lechi, a donkey's jawbone, unclean and improbable, with which a thousand fall, and the place is named Ramath-lehi in memory; the LORD saves by weak and unlikely means. And at the end Samson himself renames the whole affair: it was God's teshuah, this great deliverance, accomplished through Your servant, verse 18. In one word the killing is reframed as salvation and Samson's boast collapses into dependence, for the man who slew a thousand cannot even make water and must cry to the God who gave him everything.

Two further plays on words mark the poem Samson recites over his kill in verse 16. The Hebrew behind piled them into heaps and made them into donkeys is a single word, spelled and pronounced identically whether it means heap or donkey, so that Samson's victory boast puns on his own unlikely weapon in the very words he uses to describe the slaughter, an untranslatable joke the BSB footnote preserves by noting the alternate reading. The place name Ramath-lehi, the hill of the jawbone, verse 17, keeps that pun alive geographically, welding the weapon permanently into the landscape's memory. Even the description of the ropes snapping, like burnt flax, verse 14, reclaims the chapter's opening image of destructive fire for something entirely different; where fire earlier consumed grain and then a woman and her father, here it becomes only a simile for how easily bonds fall away before the Spirit, turning the motif that has driven the whole tragedy into a picture, at last, of effortless deliverance rather than further loss, fire unmaking in a moment what fire itself had spent two whole scenes destroying.

typology.type: The deliverer bound and handed over by his own frightened people, Judges 15:12-13
typology.fulfillment: Three thousand men of Judah, more afraid of Philistine reprisal than eager for freedom, tie up the very man raised to save them and march him toward the enemy camp, new ropes on his wrists, verse 13. Centuries later Israel's own leaders will hand over a greater Deliverer to a foreign power for similar reasons, preferring an uneasy peace with Rome to the risk His mission posed, and Peter can say in the same breath that lawless hands killed Him and that God's own plan stood behind it, Acts 2:23. The correspondence is real but the outcome is reversed: Samson's binding ends in a battle he alone survives, while Christ's ends in a death from which He alone rises.

typology.type: A weapon beneath contempt used to win an impossible victory, Judges 15:15-16
typology.fulfillment: An unclean animal's jawbone, not a sword or spear, becomes the instrument of Israel's deliverance, so that no one watching could credit Samson's own preparation for the win. Paul draws the same principle out fully when he says God chose what is foolish and weak in the world to shame the wise and the strong, 1 Corinthians 1:27, and the cross itself, an instrument of shame, becomes the very weapon by which the true enemy is defeated, Colossians 2:15. The type is only a hint, since a jawbone kills for a day while the cross secures a rescue that never needs repeating.

typology.type: A desperate cry answered with water that revives the dying, Judges 15:18-19
typology.fulfillment: At the very height of his triumph Samson is nearly undone by ordinary thirst, and only a cry to the LORD, not his own strength, opens the hollow rock that saves him. Jesus later stands at a feast and cries out that whoever is thirsty may come to Him and drink, promising streams of living water to everyone who believes, John 7:37-38, and at the cross He Himself cries I am thirsty before His work is finished, John 19:28, taking on the very thirst He offers to satisfy in others. The type is dim but real: En-hakkore answers one man's thirst once, while Christ answers the thirst of everyone who calls on Him, forever.

study.christ:
This chapter is less a straight portrait of Christ than a study in what a deliverer without Christ's character looks like, and the gap between the two teaches as much as any similarity. Samson's whole campaign runs on a single sworn purpose, I will not rest until I have taken vengeance upon you, verse 7, exactly the posture Scripture elsewhere reserves for God alone, vengeance is Mine, I will repay, Deuteronomy 32:35. Christ never claims that reservation for Himself. Struck, mocked, and finally nailed to a cross, He does not vow retaliation but intercession, Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing, Luke 23:34, taking onto Himself the very wrath that Samson spends the whole chapter trying to inflict on someone else.

Yet the chapter is not only contrast. Its middle scene, in which Samson's own countrymen bind him with new ropes and hand him to the Philistines to keep an uneasy peace, verse 13, anticipates a deeper irony that will recur at Christ's trial: a people more anxious to avoid trouble with a ruling power than to stand with the one sent to save them. Samson goes willingly to that binding once he has secured a promise that his own people will not kill him themselves, verse 12; Christ goes to His binding having secured no such promise, submitting to a death His own people actively call for.

The chapter's final scene, thirst met with water from a rock the LORD splits open, verse 19, sits alongside a whole line of texts where Christ offers Himself as the answer to human thirst, streams of living water flowing from within everyone who believes, John 7:37-38, and, on the cross itself, taking on the thirst of every dying sinner as His own, I am thirsty, John 19:28. Samson receives water so his own strength can return for a further, private act of revenge; Christ gives water so that others may never thirst again, asking nothing back for Himself.
study.god:
God's patience in this chapter extends in two directions at once, toward Samson's temper and toward Judah's fear, and neither one earns what it receives. He does not rebuke the three thousand men of Judah for their willingness to hand over a deliverer rather than fight for their own freedom, nor does He strike Samson for a campaign of retaliation that Scripture elsewhere reserves for God's own hand alone, Deuteronomy 32:35. Instead He works through both failures toward a single outcome, the Philistine grip on Judah's hill country broken for a season, showing a governance that does not wait for its instruments to become worthy before using them.

There is also a boundary to notice in how God acts here. The chapter could easily have kept escalating, fire for fire, death for death, yet it comes to rest at a fixed point, a slaughter that ends the immediate threat rather than spiraling into full scale war, as though the LORD sets a limit on how far this particular cycle of vengeance is allowed to run. That restraint says something true about God even where the text never states it outright: He can use violent times and violent men for His purposes without those purposes being open ended license for unlimited violence.

Above all this chapter shows a God who hears an imperfect prayer. Samson's cry mixes a genuine acknowledgment, you have accomplished this great deliverance through your servant, with an anxious, almost accusing question, must I now die of thirst, verse 18, and God answers the whole of it, mixed motives and all, exactly as the Psalter later promises, this poor man cried and the LORD heard him, He saved him from all his troubles, Psalm 34:6. The spring that opens at Lehi becomes, in the narrator's own words, a place that remains to this day, verse 19, a small but deliberate note that God's care for one exhausted man was written down to be remembered by people who would never meet him.

crossReferences.note: Moses declares in his closing song that vengeance and repayment belong to the LORD alone, precisely the territory Samson steps into when he swears, I will not rest until I have taken vengeance, verse 7. The law itself supplies the standard by which Samson's zeal, however understandable, still falls short.

Paul quotes this very principle from Deuteronomy as direct instruction to believers, never avenge yourselves, but leave room for God's wrath. Samson's chapter shows what it costs when a deliverer takes that role onto himself instead of leaving it to the God who alone can wield it justly.

God chooses what is foolish and weak in the world to shame the wise and the strong, exactly the logic behind an unclean donkey's jawbone becoming the weapon of Israel's deliverance. Neither text lets the instrument of victory receive any of the glory that belongs to the one who chose it.

Jesus stands at a feast and cries that anyone thirsty may come to Him and drink, promising streams of living water for all who believe. Samson's thirst is met once, from a single rock, for a single man; Christ's promise is for everyone, for as long as anyone comes.

The occasion the LORD had already been seeking against the Philistines through Samson's marriage, revealed to the reader alone in chapter 14, comes to its first open harvest here, as private grievance widens into public deliverance. What began as one man's demand becomes, without his full understanding, the LORD's method of finally striking the oppressor.

This poor man cried out, and the LORD heard him and saved him from all his troubles, the exact shape of Samson's cry at Lehi, an exhausted man crying honestly and being answered, regardless of how mixed his motives may have been.

When Israel once tried to fight in its own strength after refusing to trust God, Moses warned them not to go up, for the LORD is not among you, and they were struck down. Samson's victory shows the opposite case, an outnumbered man who wins precisely because the LORD's Spirit, not human numbers, fights through him.

Generations later Israel's whole army stands paralyzed before a single Philistine champion until one young man steps forward in the LORD's strength instead of the nation's own. The same pattern that saves Judah through Samson alone saves Israel again through David alone, a single deliverer standing where a frightened people will not.

Samson is remembered among those who through faith quenched the power of fire and became mighty in battle, only a chapter after his own foxes had wielded fire to devastating effect. The list in Hebrews does not sanitize his record; it simply insists that God's power, not Samson's character, is the point being commended.

study.oneStory:
Since Cain struck down Abel in the world's first act of personal violence, Genesis 4:8, human beings have carried an instinct for retaliation that the fall unleashed and that the law was later given partly to restrain, an eye for eye rather than an unlimited spiral of vengeance, Exodus 21:24. Judges 15 shows that instinct running at full speed, one household's grievance metastasizing within a few verses into an international war, until an entire tribe would rather surrender its own champion than risk the fighting spreading further. The chapter is therefore a small, sharp picture of what fallen human relationships default to whenever grace does not intervene.

But grace does intervene, and it intervenes through the very mess rather than around it. The LORD does not wait for Samson's motives to purify themselves before empowering him; the Spirit comes mightily upon him in the middle of a revenge campaign, and the deliverance Israel receives that day is every bit as real for having arrived by so compromised a channel. This is the same God who will, at far greater cost, use the worst act of injustice in history, the unjust killing of His own innocent Son, as the very means of saving the world, so that Samson's tangled, half righteous victory becomes one more small rehearsal of a much larger pattern.

The chapter ends, fittingly, not with a victory speech but with a thirsty man's prayer, a reminder that even the deliverer who kills a thousand cannot supply his own next breath of life. That posture, empty handed dependence after the greatest of triumphs, is where every human deliverer, however Spirit filled, must eventually arrive, and where the true and final Deliverer never had to, since His strength, unlike Samson's, never needed refilling from outside Himself, John 5:26.

quiz.q: What set off the chain of revenge in this chapter?

options.text: Samson's wife had been given to another man, so he burned the Philistines' harvest, and the cycle escalated from there.
options.note: Verses 1-5 show the lost wife leading Samson to burn the fields, igniting the retaliation.

options.text: The Philistines attacked Samson's home without any provocation.
options.note: There was conflict, but the chapter traces the spiral back to the lost wife and the burned fields.

options.text: The men of Judah started a war against the Philistines.
options.note: Judah did the opposite; they tried to hand Samson over to keep the peace.

options.text: God commanded Samson to take personal revenge.
options.note: Scripture reserves vengeance for God; Samson acted on his own grievance.

quiz.q: How did the men of Judah respond to the Philistine threat?

options.text: They bound their own deliverer and handed him over, resigned to Philistine rule.
options.note: Verses 11-13 show Judah's shameful passivity, binding Samson to keep the peace.

options.text: They rallied behind Samson to fight for their freedom.
options.note: The opposite: they were content in bondage and delivered Samson to the enemy.

options.text: They asked Samson to lead them into battle.
options.note: They came not to enlist him but to arrest him and hand him over.

options.text: They fled the region entirely.
options.note: They stayed and negotiated the surrender of Samson, not flight.

quiz.q: With what did Samson strike down a thousand Philistines?

options.text: The fresh jawbone of a donkey, after the Spirit of the LORD rushed on him.
options.note: Verses 14-15 credit the Spirit and the improbable weapon of a donkey's jawbone.

options.text: A sword he took from a fallen Philistine.
options.note: He used a jawbone, not a sword; the weakness of the weapon is the point.

options.text: His bare hands alone.
options.note: He broke his ropes by the Spirit, but he took up a jawbone to strike them down.

options.text: The help of the three thousand men of Judah.
options.note: Judah had bound him; he fought alone as the Spirit empowered him.

quiz.q: What did Samson do when he was dying of thirst after the battle?

options.text: He cried out to the LORD, naming the victory God's deliverance, and God opened a spring to revive him.
options.note: Verses 18-19 show his prayer of dependence and God's merciful provision of water.

options.text: He found a well and drew water by his own strength.
options.note: He had no strength left for that; God had to open the spring in answer to prayer.

options.text: He demanded that Judah bring him water.
options.note: He turned to God in prayer, not to the men who had bound him.

options.text: He gave up and prepared to die.
options.note: He did not give up; he called on the LORD, who answered.

quiz.q: How does Samson in this chapter point us to Christ?

options.text: He is handed over by his own people yet brings deliverance, foreshadowing Christ, though Christ conquers by bearing vengeance rather than taking it.
options.note: Samson points to Christ by likeness and contrast; Christ saves through His death, not slaughter.

options.text: He shows that taking personal revenge is the way to serve God.
options.note: His Spirit-empowered deliverance is real, but his personal vengeance is a warning, not a model.

options.text: He proves God only saves through strong and impressive means.
options.note: The opposite: a jawbone and a spring show God saving by weakness.

options.text: He has no connection to Christ whatsoever.
options.note: As a deliverer handed over by his own who yet brings rescue, he clearly foreshadows Christ.

questions: The whole chapter is a spiral of revenge, each blow provoking the next. Where is a desire to get even quietly taking root in you, and what would it mean to leave vengeance to God?
Judah was so at home in bondage that they bound their own deliverer. Are there chains you have made peace with rather than longing to be free?
God won a great deliverance through an unclean, improbable jawbone. How does it encourage you that God delights to save through weak and unlikely means, including you?
At his strongest moment Samson was helpless with thirst and had to cry to God. Where do you need to admit that your gifts and successes still leave you utterly dependent on the Lord?
En-hakkore means the spring of him who calls, and Christ gives living water to the thirsty. What thirst are you carrying to Him this week to drink and be revived?

translationNotes.note: Struck them ruthlessly renders a Hebrew idiom the BSB footnote gives as literally he struck them hip and thigh, a vivid phrase for a thorough, devastating slaughter.
Deployed themselves near Lehi carries a BSB footnote reading literally and spread out in Lehi; Lehi means jawbone, anticipating the weapon and the naming of Ramath-lehi.
I have piled them into heaps involves a Hebrew wordplay on donkey and heap; the BSB footnote notes the line can also read I have made them into donkeys.
En-hakkore, as the BSB footnote explains, means the spring of him who calls, memorializing Samson's answered cry to the LORD.
